plan.title: Marie Curie: The Woman Who Won Two Nobel Prizes
plan.description: Marie Curie went from a poor student in Paris to the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. This video follows her discovery of polonium and radium, her work in World War I, and the cost of her research.

beats.narration: She lived on buttered bread and tea. Her health sometimes suffered. Yet this student would become the first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes. How did Marie Curie get there?

props.title: Marie Curie
props.subtitle: From buttered bread and tea to two Nobel Prizes

beats.chapter: A poor student with a big question

beats.narration: She was born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw on November 7, 1867. Her father was a secondary-school teacher, and he gave her some early scientific training.
Warsaw was then part of Poland dominated by Russia. After joining a students' revolutionary organization, she found it wise to leave for Cracow.
In 1891 she finally reached Paris and enrolled at the Sorbonne. With little money, she threw herself into study. She finished a physics degree in 1893, and a mathematics degree the next year.
In 1894 she met Pierre Curie, a professor of physics. They married the next year. Together they would change science.
Uranium gave off rays. Marie tested other elements and found that thorium did too. She concluded that radiation comes from atoms themselves, not from how they are arranged in molecules.
In 1898 the Curies announced two new elements. First came polonium, named for her native Poland. Then radium, from the Latin word for ray. Marie called this natural glow radioactivity.

props.alt: The periodic table and old laboratory glassware

beats.narration: Proving it was brutal. From a tonne of pitchblende, they separated only one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride. It took Marie over three years.

props.label: Radium chloride from one tonne of pitchblende

beats.narration: In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Henri Becquerel for their work on radioactivity. Marie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
Then tragedy struck. In 1906 Pierre was hit by a horse-drawn cart in Paris and died. Marie took his place as professor at the Sorbonne, the first woman ever to hold that post.
In 1910 she isolated pure radium metal. In 1911 she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry. No one had ever won twice.

props.text: The first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes.

beats.narration: During World War I, she directed the Red Cross Radiology Service. Her X-ray work reached about one million soldiers.

props.label: Soldiers received X-rays through her Red Cross service

beats.narration: Radiation had a cost. Marie died in 1934 of aplastic anemia, likely caused by years of exposure to radiation.
Her work still shapes radiology and medicine today. Her lesson is simple: patient, stubborn curiosity can change the world. Next time you see an X-ray, remember her.

props.text: Patient curiosity can change the world.

accuracy.reason: Core dates and facts match the notes. Minor slips: the Nobel Prize 'for their work' attribution, 'Marie called this natural glow radioactivity', and the degree years (the 1894 degree is described as a mathematics degree, while the NobelPrize source gives a licenciateship).

coverage.reason: It hits all the checklist items, but it omits her Polish identity beyond polonium, the radium industry and the mobile 'little Curies' X-ray vans, the 1934 death date detail, and the second prize controversy. Depth is thin for the length.

structure.reason: The chronological order is clear and chaptered, and the hook is paid off in the ending. Beat 9 says 'first woman to win a Nobel Prize' before the timeline moves on, and Pierre's death is placed after the 1903 prize, which is fine.

hook_ending.reason: The opening 'She lived on buttered bread and tea' is concrete and curious. The ending 'Next time you see an X-ray, remember her' lands, though the moral is a little stock.

tone.reason: The register is clear and suits a general audience, with short punchy sentences.

visuals.reason: The mix of scene types is varied. But the uranium-to-thorium diagram is a weak fit, the generic 'scientist working in laboratory' clip for her death is mismatched, and the bullets scene lists daughters that are never narrated.

originality.reason: Buttered bread and the tonne of pitchblende yielding a tenth of a gram are good details. Much of the rest is a standard recap of the notes.

instructions.reason: English, about the right length, covering the requested points. It is somewhat short on narrative and personal story.

language.reason: The grammar is clean and the phrasing natural.

defects.quote: Proving it was brutal. From a tonne of pitchblende, they separated only one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride. It took Marie over three years.
defects.issue: This was 1902, and the three-year effort is attributed to Marie alone. The notes frame it as the work of both Curies with industrial help.

defects.issue: The mobile 'little Curie' X-ray vans and her own driving are omitted, even though they are the most vivid wartime detail.
